questions.q: Why can `df.memory_usage(deep=False)` significantly understate a DataFrame's real memory footprint?
options: It only measures the index, not the columns
For object (string) columns, it reports the size of the pointers rather than the actual string contents
It only works on DataFrames with fewer than 1000 rows
It rounds all sizes down to the nearest megabyte
questions.explain: Without deep=True, memory_usage reports the size of the object pointers for string columns, not the strings themselves, which can massively understate true memory use.

questions.q: What does `pd.read_csv(path, chunksize=250_000)` return, and what is the typical processing pattern?
options: The entire file loaded as one DataFrame, just slower
An iterator of smaller DataFrames; you process and reduce each chunk, then merge the partial results
A single row at a time, like .iterrows()
A DataFrame with only the first 250,000 rows, discarding the rest
questions.explain: chunksize makes read_csv return an iterator of DataFrames. The standard pattern is to aggregate each chunk (e.g. groupby + sum) and merge the partial results, so the full file is never held in memory at once.

Always converts to int8 regardless of the data's range
questions.explain: downcast="integer" finds the smallest integer dtype (e.g. int16 instead of int64) that still losslessly represents every value in the column, reducing memory use.

questions.q: Why does converting a ticker column with only a few distinct values to `category` dtype save so much memory?
options: category compresses the DataFrame using gzip internally
It stores each unique string value once and represents every row as a small integer code pointing at it, instead of storing a full string per row
category dtype deletes duplicate rows automatically
It converts the column to a NumPy array with no index
questions.explain: category dtype stores the small set of unique values once and encodes each row as a compact integer code referencing one of them, which is dramatically cheaper than storing a full Python string per row.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the recommended order of operations when a dataset seems too large for pandas?
options: Immediately switch to a distributed cluster, skipping pandas entirely
Try chunked reading, dtype downcasting, and category conversion first (they're nearly free); only reach for an out-of-core engine if the data still doesn't fit
Always rewrite the pipeline in a different programming language first
Delete rows at random until the file fits in memory
questions.explain: The lesson's rule of thumb is to try the nearly-free techniques (chunking, downcasting, category) first since they often yield a 3-10x reduction, and only move to an out-of-core or distributed engine if the data still doesn't fit after that.
